sentences.text: Adult Hongshanornis longicresta measured roughly the size of a thrush, weighing about 50 grams with a wingspan of approximately 320 millimeters.
The total wing area of this bird was 0.016 square meters.
Among its toes, the third was the longest.
Fossil evidence shows the bird possessed at least 10 tail feathers, a number greater than seen in other primitive fan-tailed birds.
Researchers identified a distinct bone at the lower jaw's tip, comparing it to the predentary bone found in ornithischian dinosaurs.
While initial descriptions proposed a large feathered crest, a second specimen displayed shorter feathers near the snout, implying the original feature might be a preservation artifact.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the primary reference for the species, was recovered in 2005 and is now held by the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology in Beijing.
One preserved individual contained gizzard stones, suggesting an herbivorous diet.
The absence of slots in the wings indicates the bird likely flew at relatively high speeds.
Hongshanornis likely flapped continuously at low speeds and switched to bounding flight at higher speeds.
This species is the namesake of the family Hongshanornithidae.
Hongshanornis is an ornithuromorph bird known from early Cretaceous lake deposits in the Yixian Formation of Inner Mongolia, China.
Fossils were found in the Jianshangou fossil beds, which are dated to 124.6 million years ago.
The time range for Hongshanornis spans from the Barremian to the Aptian, between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago.
It is debated whether Hongshanornis possessed a beak, as some scientists argue its jaw bone lacks the characteristic pits and grooves found in early beaked birds.
